memory-hierarchy.name: The memory hierarchy
memory-hierarchy.oneLine: Registers, caches, DRAM and disk differ in latency by factors of ten to a million, and every performance question is really about which one you are talking to.

readings.title: Latency numbers every programmer should know
What Every Programmer Should Know About Memory

cache-lines.name: Cache lines and blocks
cache-lines.oneLine: A cache never moves a byte; it moves a whole line, typically 64 bytes, so touching one byte brings its neighbours along for free.

readings.title: What Every Programmer Should Know About Memory

spatial-locality.name: Spatial locality and stride
spatial-locality.oneLine: Walking memory in small steps reuses lines already fetched; walking in steps larger than a line throws most of every fetch away.

virtual-memory.name: Virtual memory
virtual-memory.oneLine: Each process sees its own address space, and the hardware translates those addresses to physical frames through page tables the kernel maintains.

paging.name: Pages and page tables
paging.oneLine: Memory is managed in fixed-size pages, usually 4 KiB, and a multi-level page table maps virtual page numbers to physical frame numbers.

readings.title: Five-level page tables
readings.where: Linux kernel docs, for how deep it really goes

mmu-tlb.name: The MMU and the TLB
mmu-tlb.oneLine: Address translation is done in hardware by the MMU, and the TLB caches recent translations so that most memory accesses do not need a page-table walk at all.

page-faults.name: Page faults
page-faults.oneLine: When a translation is missing or forbidden the MMU raises a fault, the kernel decides whether it is legitimate, and the faulting instruction is re-run as though nothing happened.

readings.title: Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces
readings.where: Ch. 21–22, swapping and the fault path

readings.title: The Linux Programming Interface
readings.where: Ch. 49 on mmap, for what a fault does to a mapping

cap-theorem.name: Partitions, consistency and availability
cap-theorem.oneLine: A network partition forces a choice between refusing to answer and answering from possibly stale state; the rest of the time the trade-off is latency, not availability.

readings.title: Designing Data-Intensive Applications
readings.where: Ch. 9, especially the critique of CAP

readings.title: Please stop calling databases CP or AP

replication.name: Replication
replication.oneLine: The same data is kept on several nodes so that one can fail without losing it, which immediately raises the question of what to do when copies disagree.

array-bounds.name: Array bounds and off-by-one
array-bounds.oneLine: C and C++ do not check indexes, so reading one element past the end is undefined behaviour that usually looks like it worked.

readings.title: Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective
readings.where: Ch. 3.10, buffer overflows and why they are exploitable

sanitizers.name: Sanitizers
sanitizers.oneLine: AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer instrument your program at compile time so that memory errors and undefined behaviour fail loudly instead of appearing to work.

readings.title: AddressSanitizer
readings.where: the flags, and how to read a report

readings.title: UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer
readings.where: the list of checks it can make

alignment.name: Alignment and padding
alignment.oneLine: A type must sit at an address that is a multiple of its alignment, so the compiler inserts padding between struct members and at the end of the struct.

readings.title: The Lost Art of Structure Packing
readings.where: Eric S. Raymond, the definitive walkthrough

pipelining.name: Instruction pipelining and hazards
pipelining.oneLine: A CPU overlaps the stages of consecutive instructions, and a hazard is any case where the overlap would use a value that is not ready yet.

readings.title: Digital Design and Computer Architecture
readings.where: Harris & Harris, ch. 7.5, with the five-stage diagrams

amdahl.name: Amdahl's law
amdahl.oneLine: Speedup from parallelism is bounded by the fraction of the work that stays serial, so a 5% serial part caps you at 20x however many cores you buy.

readings.title: Introduction to High Performance Computing for Scientists and Engineers
Amdahl's Law in the Multicore Era
readings.where: Hill & Marty, short and worth it

readings.title: MIT 6.172 Performance Engineering
readings.where: Lecture 1, on what to expect from parallelism

cache-coherence.name: Cache coherence and false sharing
cache-coherence.oneLine: Cores keep coherent copies of a cache line, so two threads writing different variables that share a line fight over it even though they never touch the same byte.

readings.title: What Every Programmer Should Know About Memory
cppreference: hardware_destructive_interference_size
readings.where: the standard's own name for a cache line

stdio-buffering.name: stdio buffering
stdio-buffering.oneLine: The C library buffers output in your process's own memory and decides when to call write(2), and the policy depends on whether the destination is a terminal.

readings.title: man setvbuf
readings.where: the three modes, and how to change them

readings.title: Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective
readings.where: Ch. 10, on the gap between stdio and the syscalls

processes-fork.name: Processes and fork
processes-fork.oneLine: fork() creates a near-identical copy of the calling process, which continues from the same point with its own copy of everything the parent had.

readings.title: man fork
readings.where: especially the long list of what is and is not inherited

copy-on-write.name: Copy-on-write
copy-on-write.oneLine: fork() does not copy memory; it marks both processes' pages read-only and shared, and copies a page only when one of them writes to it.

readings.where: Ch. 23, on the VM system's lazy tricks

readings.title: Linux memory accounting
readings.where: proc(5): statm, smaps and what RSS actually counts

mutual-exclusion.name: Locks and deadlock
mutual-exclusion.oneLine: A mutex makes a critical section exclusive, and two threads taking two mutexes in opposite orders can each hold what the other needs.

readings.title: Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces
readings.where: Ch. 28 and 32, locks and concurrency bugs

readings.title: cppreference: std::scoped_lock
readings.where: the all-at-once alternative to nested lock_guards

scheduling.name: CPU scheduling
scheduling.oneLine: The scheduler decides which runnable task gets the CPU next, trading average turnaround time against response time and fairness.

readings.title: CFS scheduler design
readings.where: Linux kernel docs, on virtual runtime

readings.title: Systems Performance
readings.where: Gregg, ch. 6, for how to observe scheduling in practice

file-permissions.name: File permissions and modes
file-permissions.oneLine: Every file carries three sets of three bits — read, write, execute for owner, group and others — plus setuid, setgid and the sticky bit.

shell-pipelines.name: Pipelines and text tools
shell-pipelines.oneLine: Each tool reads a stream and writes a stream, and a pipeline composes them into something none of them does alone.

readings.title: The Unix Programming Environment
readings.where: Kernighan & Pike, ch. 4 — still the best thing on this

readings.title: Command-line Tools can be 235x Faster than your Hadoop Cluster
readings.where: Adam Drake, for a sense of scale

file-descriptors.name: File descriptors and redirection
file-descriptors.oneLine: A file descriptor is a small integer indexing a per-process table of open files, and redirection is the shell rewriting entries in that table before it execs your program.

readings.title: Bash Reference Manual: Redirections
readings.where: the order of operations is the part to read

dynamic-linking.name: Dynamic linking and the loader
dynamic-linking.oneLine: A dynamically linked program names the shared libraries it needs, and the loader finds them at startup by searching a defined list of places.

readings.title: man ld.so
readings.where: the search order, which is the part worth knowing

readings.title: How To Write Shared Libraries
readings.where: Drepper, for what the loader is really doing

syscall-tracing.name: Tracing syscalls
syscall-tracing.oneLine: strace shows every system call a process makes with its arguments and its result, which turns 'it does not work' into a specific failing call.

readings.title: strace Wow Much Syscall
readings.where: Julia Evans, the friendliest introduction there is

readings.title: Systems Performance
readings.where: Gregg, ch. 5, on tracing tools and their costs

cgroups-oom.name: cgroups and the OOM killer
cgroups-oom.oneLine: A cgroup caps a group of processes' memory, and exceeding it invokes the OOM killer inside that group rather than on the machine as a whole.

readings.title: Control Group v2
readings.where: kernel docs, the memory controller section

compilation-pipeline.name: The compilation pipeline
compilation-pipeline.oneLine: Source becomes a running program through a fixed sequence of translations, and knowing which stage you are at tells you which tool to reach for.

readings.title: Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective
readings.where: Ch. 1.2 and ch. 7, compilation and linking

lexing.name: Lexing and tokens
lexing.oneLine: A lexer turns a flat stream of characters into a stream of tokens, which is the first point at which the text has any structure at all.

readings.title: Crafting Interpreters
readings.where: Ch. 4, scanning — the clearest treatment there is

integer-conversions.name: Integer promotions and conversions
integer-conversions.oneLine: C promotes small integer types to int before arithmetic, and when the operands differ it converts them by a fixed ranking that can turn a signed value unsigned.

readings.title: Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective
readings.where: Ch. 2.2.5 and 2.3, signed and unsigned conversion

readings.where: the usual arithmetic conversions, spelled out

undefined-behaviour.name: Undefined behaviour
undefined-behaviour.oneLine: Some operations have no defined meaning at all, which licenses the optimiser to assume they never happen and to delete the code that would only matter if they did.

readings.title: What Every C Programmer Should Know About Undefined Behavior
Undefined Behavior: What Happened to My Code?
readings.where: Wang et al., with real examples from real projects

roofline.name: The roofline model
roofline.oneLine: A kernel's arithmetic intensity — flops per byte moved — decides whether it is limited by the machine's compute throughput or by its memory bandwidth.

readings.title: Roofline: An Insightful Visual Performance Model
readings.where: Williams, Waterman & Patterson — the original, and readable

readings.title: Introduction to High Performance Computing for Scientists and Engineers

row-major.name: Row-major layout and loop order
row-major.oneLine: C stores a 2D array one row at a time, so the rightmost index is the one that walks contiguously through memory and the loop order has to match.

readings.title: What Every Programmer Should Know About Memory
Cache Blocking Techniques
readings.where: Intel, on tiling once the order is right

prefix-sum.name: Prefix sum (scan)
prefix-sum.oneLine: A scan turns a sequence into its running totals, and despite looking irreducibly sequential it parallelises to logarithmic depth — which makes it the building block of a surprising number of parallel algorithms.

collectives.name: Collective communication
collectives.oneLine: A collective is an operation every rank in a group takes part in together, and each one has a characteristic communication pattern and cost.

readings.title: Introduction to High Performance Computing for Scientists and Engineers
Optimization of Collective Communication Operations in MPICH
readings.where: Thakur et al., for how they are actually implemented

tiling.name: Tiling and blocking
tiling.oneLine: Restructuring a loop nest to work on blocks small enough to stay in cache, so that data loaded once is used many times before it is evicted.

readings.title: Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective
readings.where: Ch. 6.6, and the matmul case study

readings.title: Cache-Oblivious Algorithms
readings.where: Frigo et al., for the version that needs no tile size

logical-clocks.name: Logical clocks
logical-clocks.oneLine: A Lamport clock is a counter per process, incremented on each event and advanced on receipt to exceed the sender's, which gives an ordering consistent with causality without any synchronised time.

readings.title: Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System
readings.where: Lamport, 1978 — short, and the foundation of everything after it
